processing: A cultivar rather than a method: the leaf is suited to black tea, green tea and pu-erh, and each follows its own usual processing.
harvest_season: Spring buds appear in early March, and the one-bud-three-leaf flush peaks in late March or early April.
appearance_dry: As a raw material the large leaves dry into long, thick strands; made as raw pu-erh they are typically dark green with pale tips.
appearance_liquor: As raw pu-erh, typically a clear golden yellow; as black tea the same leaf gives a red-orange cup.
appearance_wet: Broad elliptical green leaves, large and thick, opening fully.
taste_profile: This is a plant rather than a finished tea, so the cup depends on the craft; large-leaf Yunnan raw tea is typically full and brisk with some bitterness, and the black tea made from it is known as Dian Hong.

brewing.notes: These figures suit it made as raw pu-erh. Keep early steeps short, because large-leaf material turns bitter fast. For Dian Hong made from this leaf, use a little cooler water.

vintage_note: Rarely sold under its own name. You meet it as the leaf behind Dian Hong and behind Yunnan raw and green teas, labelled by origin or by factory. As pu-erh it follows the usual rule of sale by harvest year; as black tea, the current year or the one or two after it is usual.
description:
Fengqing Dayecha is a tea plant, not a finished tea: a large-leaf variety from Fengqing County in Yunnan, listed nationally as an improved variety in China. It is best known as the leaf that launched Dian Hong, Yunnan's black tea.

It is seed-propagated, so a field holds a population of related plants instead of one clone. The trees grow tall with high branching and sparse growth, the leaves are very large and elliptical, and it buds early, with spring buds in early March and the one-bud-three-leaf flush peaking in late March or early April. It also tolerates cold better than Mengku or Menghai large-leaf.

The same leaf can go into black, green or pu-erh tea, so there is no single flavour to learn. What it brings, as is typical of Yunnan big-leaf plants, is weight and strength in the cup. Brew short at first.

You will seldom see the variety on a label. If a seller names it, ask what tea was actually made from it, and where in Yunnan or beyond it grew, since it is also planted in Sichuan, Guizhou, Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan and Hunan.
history:
Tea drinking in Fengqing has an early literary trace: the traveller Xu Xiake reached the county in the eighth month of 1639 and wrote of a host brewing him Taihua tea. That entry concerns local tea, and it does not identify this variety.

The plant's modern fame dates from 1938, when the Nationalist government sent Feng Shaoqiu to Yunnan's tea areas to try black tea production for foreign exchange during the war against Japan. He found this leaf made the best black tea, and from that work came Dian Hong.

In 1985 China's national crop variety committee recognised it as a national variety.
